hooks.text: To survive the first spacewalk, Alexei Leonov had to bleed his oxygen.
Why did the first spacewalker have to deflate his own suit?
The first man to walk in space was trapped outside his ship.

title: The Spacewalker Trapped Outside His Ship
description: In 1965, Alexei Leonov became the first human to walk in space, but his suit ballooned in the vacuum, nearly trapping him outside.

beats.text: To survive the first spacewalk, Alexei Leonov had to bleed his oxygen.
beats.visual: Alexei Leonov performing the first spacewalk outside Voskhod 2, 1965

beats.text: On March 18, 1965, the Soviet mission Voskhod 2 reached orbit with Leonov and commander Pavel Belyayev.
beats.visual: Alexei Leonov and Pavel Belyayev crew portrait, 1965

beats.text: Roughly 90 minutes after launch, Leonov floated into the vacuum, tethered only by a slender line.
beats.visual: Alexei Leonov floating outside the spacecraft tethered by a line, 1965

beats.text: But after 12 minutes outside, his suit ballooned and stiffened so much he could no longer bend his joints.
His feet slipped out of his boots, leaving him unable to pull himself back through the airlock door.
beats.visual: Voskhod 2 spacecraft model showing the Volga inflatable airlock

beats.text: Without telling ground control, Leonov opened a valve to release his life-sustaining pressure just to squeeze inside.
beats.visual: Alexei Leonov in his Berkut spacesuit prior to launch

beats.text: After a manual reentry, the crew crash-landed deep in the Ural Mountains and spent two nights among wolves and bears.
beats.visual: Snowy Siberian taiga forest near Perm representing the landing terrain

beats.text: His suit had become a pressurized trap, showing why
beats.visual: Alexei Leonov in his spacesuit post-mission portrait, 1965
